title: DHS Has Used This Controversial Investigative Tool 185,000 Times Since Trump Took Office
gist: Homeland Security Investigations estimates it has sent at least 185,000 warrantless administrative subpoenas since the Trump administration began—more than ICE's ~170,000 customs summonses over 2016–mid-2022—as revealed in an EFF FOIA lawsuit. DHS now argues its inherited customs-summons power covers a broad investigative portfolio, and tech platforms like Google and Reddit face compelled-disclosure pressure.

insights.claim: Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE's investigative wing, estimates in a court filing that it has sent at least 185,000 administrative subpoenas since the start of the Trump administration.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Tech platforms, ISPs and service providers face a sharply elevated volume of warrantless government data requests, with compliance and trust costs.
insights.locator: Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative wing

insights.claim: HSI's estimate of 185,000 administrative subpoenas in under two years exceeds the roughly 170,000 1509 customs summonses ICE agents sent over more than six and a half years from early 2016 to mid-August 2022.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Signals a step-change in government reliance on warrantless data demands, relevant to platform policy and privacy-product demand.
insights.locator: To put HSI’s estimate into perspective

insights.claim: The 185,000 figure surfaced in an Electronic Frontier Foundation FOIA lawsuit that originally sought counts of administrative subpoenas sent to technology companies, internet platforms and service providers; it is unclear whether the figure covers only those companies or a broader set.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Further disclosure from the litigation could quantify how much of this burden falls on tech companies specifically.
insights.locator: The number of administrative subpoenas was revealed

insights.claim: Administrative subpoenas let the government demand records from companies without explaining to any court why it needs them or what data it is requesting, unlike grand jury subpoenas or court orders.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: The lack of judicial gatekeeping makes these requests cheap to issue, so volume can scale with little friction.
insights.locator: Administrative subpoenas are a powerful but unchecked

insights.claim: Since the Trump administration began, DHS's administrative subpoena power has been used to try to unmask anonymous online critics and obtain broad customer records about protesters, including a list of Minneapolis-St. Paul buyers of a specific green beanie from REI.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Retailers and online platforms holding customer data are being drawn into politically sensitive surveillance requests, a reputational and legal risk.
insights.locator: Since the start of the Trump administration, the federal government

insights.claim: The Trump administration has reversed DHS's earlier position—reflected in a 2017 inspector general rebuke for using a customs summons to unmask a Twitter user—and now argues in court that inherited Customs Service powers can be used across its broad investigative portfolio beyond customs and immigration enforcement.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: A legal theory expanding customs summons scope would make warrantless data demands available for virtually any DHS investigation.
insights.quote: beyond legacy customs and immigration enforcement.

insights.claim: EFF's Aaron Mackey argues ICE files so many administrative subpoenas because there is virtually no downside: if a platform refuses, ICE can sue to compel compliance, as it recently did with Google, or switch to a grand jury subpoena, as reportedly happened with Reddit.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Platform pushback offers limited protection; tech companies should expect litigation and escalation rather than withdrawal when they refuse.
insights.quote: The worst thing that will happen to ICE is that the service that receives it says it's not going to respond,
insights.locator: “The worst thing that will happen to ICE

insights.claim: Senator Ron Wyden called the subpoena numbers a dragnet domestic surveillance program, is pushing his bipartisan Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act, and plans to use the Senate Finance Committee gavel next year to investigate HSI's use of customs law.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Watch for congressional oversight and possible legislation curbing administrative subpoenas, which would change the compliance landscape for platforms.
insights.quote: Next year, I plan to use the Senate Finance Committee gavel to get to the bottom of HSI's unprecedented misuse of customs law to target Trump's enemies.
insights.locator: “Congress desperately needs to pass my bipartisan legislation
